claims.text: FeCoNiTi-based high-entropy alloys are rare-earth-free magnetic alloys.
A strong low-field magnetocaloric response in FeCoNiTi-based alloys is governed by magnetostructural coupling.
Chemical-disorder-induced lattice distortions tune the proposed magnetostructural coupling.
Local antiferromagnetic interactions associated with Ti substitution tune the proposed magnetostructural coupling.
The proposed coupling promotes field-induced domain reordering with a large magnetic-entropy change.
A fine, coherent microstructure containing nanoscale grain boundaries or coherent precipitates enables rapid heat exchange.
The fine, coherent microstructure provides low hysteresis and mechanical integrity.
The initial FeCoNiTi-based alloy is as-cast and chemically disordered.
The initial alloy has a dual-phase microstructure containing fcc and secondary phases.
The initial alloy is predominantly fcc with only minor secondary phases.
The fcc phase of FeCoNiTi has a low-temperature magnetic transition.
The initial alloy has low saturation magnetization because of Ti substitution.
Ti substitution enhances magnetocrystalline anisotropy in the initial alloy.
Changing Ti concentration or short-range order adjusts lattice distortions and local magnetic exchange interactions.
Ti induces local antiferromagnetic coupling with Fe, Co, and Ni atoms.
Ti-induced antiferromagnetic coupling reduces saturation magnetization and enhances magnetocrystalline anisotropy.
The magnetic effects of Ti and disorder-induced lattice distortions lower the energy barrier for field-induced domain reorientation.
The resulting transition is nearly reversible and produces a large isothermal magnetic-entropy change under fields below 1 T.
An optimized Ti level or optimized short-range order will increase both isothermal entropy change and adiabatic temperature change relative to the baseline.
The optimized alloy will have reduced magnetic hysteresis without degrading mechanical properties or thermal conductivity.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis invokes nanoscale grain boundaries as beneficial microstructural features, while the structural mediator says the nanoscale-grained microstructure minimizes interfaces. Refining grains generally increases grain-boundary interfacial area, so these descriptions are internally inconsistent without further qualification.
